item.title: AI giants agree on shared robots.txt token for publisher opt‑out
item.description:
AI giants agree on shared robots.txt token for publisher opt‑out

OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic announced they will adopt a new standard that lets publishers opt out of AI‑powered scraping via a shared signal placed in a site’s robots.txt file.

🔍 Overview

  • The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping.
  • Publishers can apply their AI training preferences across multiple crawlers instead of setting them individually.
  • The signal lives within the existing robots.txt file, which already tells crawlers what they may or may not scrape.

🧩 How it works

  • A policy token is added to robots.txt; any AI crawler that respects the standard will read the token and honor the publisher’s preferences.
  • The token was proposed by Kevin Kelley, a technical lead for standards at Anthropic, as part of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) process.
  • When a crawler encounters the token, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic say they will restrict their AI crawlers from accessing the site.

⚙️ Key details

  • Meta: Communications head Andy Stone said, “We believe creating a common signal that conveys such preferences to multiple providers at once is an important step,” and added, “And we look forward to working with other AI companies on the standards and their implementation across the industry.” Meta has signaled support but has not confirmed whether it will honor the token.
  • Microsoft: Will offer granular controls that let publishers opt out of AI training or AI grounding. Sites will still appear in Bing search results regardless of their choices.
  • Google: Previously implemented similar controls that let sites block AI search features or training without affecting search visibility.
  • Existing efforts to curb unauthorized scraping include the Really Simple Licensing (RSL) standard, which lets publishers charge crawlers, and Cloudflare’s default blocking of AI crawlers.

🚀 Availability

Company Current status Planned rollout
Anthropic Already adopted the signal –
Google Will support the signal Next year
Microsoft Will support the signal Next year
OpenAI Will implement the signal Coming months

💡 Why it matters

  • Publishers no longer need to negotiate separate AI training preferences with each AI provider.
  • A single, standards‑based token simplifies compliance and reduces the administrative burden of managing many individual requests.
  • The move comes as publishers grapple with a continuing influx of AI crawlers that feed content into large language models.
  • Providing a common opt‑out mechanism could help balance the interests of content creators with the data needs of AI developers.

#OpenAI #AITraining #RobotsTxt #Publishing #IETF

Source: The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping

item.title: Meta delays enforcement of new business terms amid publisher AI-scraping concerns
item.description:
Meta delays enforcement of new business terms amid publisher AI-scraping concerns

Meta announced a delay to the rollout of its revised business terms after worldwide publisher pushback over possible AI‑training scrapes of news sites.

🔍 Overview

  • The original effective date was October 30.
  • Enforcement has been pushed to November 20.
  • Delay is intended to give Meta time to explain what is changing and what is not.
  • Publishers warned the terms could let Meta scrape news sites for AI training.

📜 Business terms details

  • The draft terms appeared to give Meta permission to freely scrape news sites for AI training.
  • Meta later removed explicit language about “training” its products, but legal experts said the change may still allow scraping.

🗣️ Publisher and regulator response

  • The News/Media Alliance sent a letter to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg demanding revisions, citing “severe harm” to publishers.
  • Digital advertisers and publishers in the European Union and the United Kingdom urged regulators to block the new terms.
  • Publisher backlash worldwide prompted Meta to delay the terms entirely.

🤝 Meta’s statement

  • spokesperson Daniel Roberts told The Verge the November 20 start “allows more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not.”
  • Roberts added the delay will let Meta detail “how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences.”

💡 Why it matters

  • Scraping news content for AI models could affect revenue and control for publishers.
  • Robots.txt remains a tool for publishers to signal crawling preferences.
  • Regulatory attention in the EU and UK highlights growing scrutiny of large platforms’ data practices.

#Meta #AI #Publishing #Regulation

Source: Meta delays new business terms after publisher pushback on AI scraping

item.title: Google Launches Pilot Program to Pay Publishers for AI Contributions
item.description:
Google Launches Pilot Program to Pay Publishers for AI Contributions

Google has introduced a pilot program that compensates publishers for their contributions to its AI-powered search features and chatbot, according to reports from Digiday and The Information.

⚙️ Key details

  • The program began less than a year ago.
  • Approximately 100 publishers have joined the pilot.
  • Payments are based on how much content contributed to:
    • AI Overviews
    • AI Mode in Search
    • Gemini chatbot

💰 Compensation Examples

Publisher Status Reported Earnings
Joined at program start Over $1 million in a year
Joined a few months ago Around $50,000 to $60,000

💡 Why it matters

Google is facing scrutiny regarding the impact of its AI features on web traffic. This comes alongside regulatory actions:

  • In June, the UK ruled that Google must allow publishers to opt out of appearing in AI search features.
  • The European Union has opened an investigation into the impact on web traffic and ordered Google to make changes to its search engine.

#Google #AI #Publishing #Gemini #Search

Source: Google reportedly tests paying publishers for AI search results
